title: Neighbors
hookLine: the literal ones: know their names
tomorrow: what does faith at work sound like when nobody mentions God?

cards: Doorbell cameras make it easy to watch a whole street and know nobody on it. The package thief gets a nickname; the woman two doors down never gets a name at all. And Christians read the word neighbor two ways.
Is your neighbor everyone on earth, or the person next door? Both readings come from the Bible, and they pull in different directions.

teach.b: Leviticus gives the command: “thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” A lawyer asks Jesus the obvious follow-up: “And who is my neighbour?”
Jesus answers with a Samaritan, from a people John says Jews had little to do with, who stops on the road for a wounded stranger.
Then Jesus turns the question around: “Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?” The lawyer answers: “He that shewed mercy on him.”
The first view takes that and runs: neighbor has no border. Anyone in need, anywhere, of any people. Its best case: a love that stops at the edge of your own group isn't the love Jesus described.
The second view doesn't deny any of that; it guards the near. Proverbs: “better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off.”
Its best case: a love for all humanity that never learns one name on its own street can stay an idea.
And here's what's worth telling a friend: the Samaritan's mercy happens on one road, to the one person in front of him.
The widest story in the Gospels is also a very local one. Some Christians start with the world, some with the street. Both start with a face.

how: Christians read 'neighbor' both widely, as anyone in need, after the Good Samaritan, and locally, as the people next door; some churches organize street meals, welcome visits for new neighbors, or simple efforts to learn names.

o: the people of your own nation and no one else
anyone in need, and the people living right near you
only the members of your own church or faith

games.q: two readings of neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: a neighbor near, not a brother far

s: the Samaritan story means the people next door don't matter
it widens the circle; Proverbs still says a near neighbor beats a brother far off.
Jesus answers 'who is my neighbor?' with a question back
which of these three was neighbor to the man who fell among the thieves?
Christians all read neighbor only as the people next door
some start with the world, some with the street. both readings come from the Bible.

games.q: your friend says, "i love humanity. i don't need to know the people on my street." state the near-neighbor view at its best.
o: strangers far away don't count as neighbors at all.
love for everyone can stay an idea until it learns one name close by.
you only owe help to people who live on your block.
games.why: Proverbs: better a neighbor near than a brother far off. and the Samaritan's mercy happens on one road, to the one person in front of him.

practice: Listen for the sounds of the people around you: a door, a car, a voice through a wall, a dog down the block. Each one belongs to someone with a name. If you pray, hold the nearest one before God; if not, just wonder who they are.

wordCard.voice: Neighbors. Anyone in need, Jesus says; the person near, says Proverbs. Today, the literal ones, starting with a name.

orig.note: Greek: neighbor, the word in the lawyer's question in Luke 10:29.

carryVoice: Your line: the literal neighbor. Love for everyone still needs one name on your own street. Day seventeen-eighteen, done.
